chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hisham ibn Salim, from Sulayman ibn Khalid who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): A man happens to be in a wilderness of the earth on a cloudy day and he prays toward other than the Qibla. Then (the sky) clears and he comes to know that he had prayed toward other than the Qibla. How should he deal with it?
He said: If he is still within the prayer time, then let him repeat his prayer; but if the prayer time has passed, then his striving (ijtihad to determine the direction) suffices him.

key_terms.اجْتِهَاد: Independent effort/striving to determine a ruling or direction; here specifically the effort to locate the qibla direction through available signs
key_terms.الْقِبْلَة: The direction of prayer facing the Kaaba in Mecca, one of the preconditions (shurut) of valid salat
key_terms.قَفْر: Barren wilderness, uninhabited land — a context indicating the person has no landmarks or other guides for the qibla direction
key_terms.يَوْمُ الْغَيْمِ: A cloudy day — classical fiqh treats overcast conditions as a special case affecting one's ability to determine the qibla by sun position

ai.seo_question: What should one do if they prayed facing the wrong qibla direction due to cloudy weather?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) provides a jurisprudential ruling on a traveler who inadvertently prays facing the wrong direction due to cloudy weather obstructing his ability to determine the Qibla. The ruling establishes two cases: if the prayer time has not yet expired, the prayer must be repeated in the correct direction; if the time has passed, the prayer performed through sincere ijtihad (effort to determine direction) is accepted. This hadith illustrates the principle that genuine effort (ijtihad) in fulfilling religious obligations excuses a person when accurate determination is impossible, especially for travelers in unfamiliar terrain.
word_analysis: his ijtihad/striving (to determine the qibla direction)
